text_used.text: Every quotation below was checked by script against the fetched text (whitespace, curly quotes, footnote numbers and OCR spaces before punctuation normalised; case-insensitive). 143 checked lines were found letter for letter; 2 needed a note (a line-break hyphen in the 1916 Martyrology, and OCR errors in Clarke's Shorter Rule 76, read by eye). 'exact' is the text as printed. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God.
translations: Basil's letters, On the Spirit, the Hexaemeron and Jackson's Prolegomena: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8 (T&T Clark, 1895). CCEL plain text marked Public Domain: https://ccel.org/ccel/s/schaff/npnf208/cache/npnf208.txt. New Advent carries the same translation page by page.
Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43 (the funeral speech for Basil) and Letters 48, 50 and 76: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7 (1894). CCEL, Public Domain.

The Longer Rules, the Shorter Rules and the Morals: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK and Macmillan, 1925). archive.org OCR text. Published 1925, so public domain in the US since 1 January 2021. Clarke died in 1968, so it is NOT public domain in the UK or EU. The site is US-hosted; the quiz already quotes it.
Address to Young Men: F. M. Padelford, Essays on the Study and Use of Poetry by Plutarch and Basil the Great (Yale, 1902), on tertullian.org.
Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina: W. K. Lowther Clarke (SPCK, 1916), on tertullian.org. Published 1916, US public domain.

Socrates and Sozomen: NPNF 2nd series vol. 2 (1890). Theodoret and Jerome: NPNF 2nd series vol. 3 (1892). Athanasius: NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892). Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man: NPNF 2nd series vol. 5 (1893).
text_used.note: Two quiz lines (rich, surplus) are the site's OWN translations from the Greek, shown on the site as 'Our translation'. No pre-1929 English translation of Homilies 6 and 7 was found, so no public-domain English exists to quote. The Greek for both was fetched and read against the English (see where_he_stood).

born.text: Probably 329 or 330, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, today Kayseri in Turkey. Some older writers said Neocaesarea in Pontus. His family had estates in both.
born.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), 'St. Basil the Great' (J. McSorley): 'Born probably 329; died 1 January, 379.' Jackson, Prolegomena, NPNF 2-8: 'As to the date of St. Basil's birth opinions have varied between 316 and 330', settling on 329 or 330; 'Two cities, Caesarea in Cappadocia and Neocaesarea in Pontus, have both been named as his birthplace.' Merriam-Webster, 'Caesarea': '2 or Caesarea Mazaca see kayseri'. GOARCH: 'born about the end of the year 329 in Caesarea of Cappadocia'. OCA: 'born in the year 330 at Caesarea'.
born.note: Plain wording that holds: 'About 329 or 330, at Caesarea in Cappadocia (today Kayseri, Turkey).' Jackson explains the birthplace doubt: no ancient text says it outright. Merriam-Webster's biographical entry: 'Saint circa 329–379'.

grew_up.text: On the family estate in Pontus, near the river Iris, then at school in Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens. His father, also Basil, was a teacher of rhetoric. His grandmother Macrina and his father taught him the faith.
grew_up.source: Oration 43, sections 12 to 14 (his father his first teacher; schools at Caesarea, then Byzantium, then Athens); Jackson, Prolegomena (father an advocate and teacher of rhetoric; mother Emmelia); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 14 January: 'St. Macrina ... grandmother of St. Basil, whom she brought up in the Christian faith'; OCA life ('the first years of his life on an estate belonging to his parents at the River Iris')
grew_up.note: The Iris estate detail is from the OCA life, not an ancient text. Jackson's table has Basil sent from 'Annen' (Annesi) to school at Caesarea about 343.
grew_up.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: was "his grandmother Macrina and his mother Emmelia raised the children in the faith". Jackson, Prolegomena, Education: "Basil was taught the rudiments of religion by his grandmother, and by his father". The mother is not named there.

family.text: Ten children were born, five boys and five girls. One boy died young, so nine grew up: four sons and five daughters. Basil was the eldest son. Macrina, the eldest child, and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste are all counted saints, and so are his mother and grandmother.
family.source: Jackson, Prolegomena: 'Of this happy union were born ten children, five boys and five girls.' Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (Clarke 1916): 'For she had four sons and five daughters'. OCA: 'Ten children were born to the elder Basil and Emilia: five sons and five daughters. Five of them were later numbered among the saints'. 1916 Roman Martyrology: Peter of Sebaste (9 January), Macrina the elder (14 January), Gregory of Nyssa (9 March).
family.note: OCA's five saints: Basil, Macrina (19 July), Gregory of Nyssa (10 January), Peter of Sebaste (9 January), Theosebia (10 January). His mother Emilia is also on OCA's 1 January list. Naucratius, the second son, died young (Life of Macrina, 'The story of Naucratius').

died.text: 1 January 379, at Caesarea, worn out by illness and hard living. He was about 49. Some modern scholars put his death in 377 or 378.
died.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'died 1 January, 379'. Jackson's chronological table: '379. Death of Basil, Jan. 1.' Jackson's footnote: 'In the Greek Kalendar January 1, the day of the death, is observed'. GOARCH: 'departed to the Lord on the 1st of January, in 379. at the age of forty-nine.' Oration 43, section 57: 'my liver, which, as you see, is wearing me away'.
died.note: The 377/378 dating is in the fathers research ('some scholars prefer 377 or 378') and is a known modern debate (P. Maraval and others), but I did not read that scholarship. Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 116) says only 'He died in the reign of Gratianus.' Gregory of Nyssa says Basil died 'Eight years after' he became bishop (Life of Macrina).

buried.text: At Caesarea, in the tomb of his fathers. The crowds were so great that many people were crushed to death at his funeral.
buried.source: Oration 43, section 80: 'was consigned to the tomb of his fathers'; 'many souls departed along with him, from the violence of the pushing and confusion'
buried.note: The tomb is lost. The Catholic Encyclopedia says no relics are mentioned before the twelfth century, when parts of his body were 'reputed' to have been brought to Bruges by a returning Crusader.
buried.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "some" corrected to "many". Oration 43.80: "many souls departed along with him, from the violence of the pushing and confusion".

also_called.text: Basil the Great (Greek Basileios ho Megas; Russian Vasily Veliky). His own brother already calls him 'the great Basil'.
also_called.source: Life of Macrina (Clarke 1916): 'Macrina's brother, the great Basil'; GOARCH Greek page title 'Ὁ Μέγας Βασίλειος'; azbyka.ru 'Святитель Василий Великий'

also_called.text: Basil of Caesarea (the Episcopal Church's title: 'Basil of Caesarea, Bishop and Theologian'). Also Basilius (Merriam-Webster's variant).
also_called.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 14 June; Merriam-Webster, 'Basil' (biographical name), 'variants or Basilius'

also_called.text: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, with Gregory the Theologian and John Chrysostom (Orthodox, 30 January). OCA calls the three 'Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs'.
also_called.source: OCA, 30 January: 'Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs: Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom'; azbyka.ru '12 февраля - Собор Трех святителей'
also_called.note: 'Ouranophantor' (revealer of heavenly things), from his troparion, is used by Greek sources (e.g. the blog name 'Οὐρανοφάντωρ Βασίλειος') but I did not check the troparion text itself.

status.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans, and remembered by Lutherans. A Doctor of the Church to Catholics. One of the Three Holy Hierarchs to the Orthodox.
status.source: USCCB (Memorial of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, Bishops and Doctors of the Church); OCA; Church of England Common Worship; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LSB (via CPH); ELW
status.note: No caveat is needed: he was never condemned, and no church calls him merely 'Blessed'.

patron_of.text: None recorded in the sources checked.
patron_of.source: Checked: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), 1916 Martyrology, OCA, GOARCH, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
patron_of.note: Popular websites list 'hospital administrators, reformers, monks, Cappadocia, Russia' and others with no source. Leave 'Patron of' out, as the Martin rule says ('ONLY with a source').

in_art.text: A thin bishop with a long, dark, pointed beard, in white vestments marked with crosses, holding a book or a scroll. Gregory says people copied 'his paleness, his beard, his gait'.
in_art.source: Oration 43, section 77: 'his paleness, his beard, his gait, his thoughtful, and generally meditative, hesitation in speaking'; the two pictures chosen for the page (Novgorod icon, Herrera painting); Catholic Encyclopedia (1909), 'Doctors of the Church': 'Doctors should be represented with books in their hands' (Durandus)
in_art.note: The description of icons is my own reading of the pictures, which is safe to print as a caption but is not from an icon-painters' manual. Dionysius of Fourna's Painter's Manual was not checked (the English translation is copyrighted).

wrote.text: Letters (366 under his name, about 325 genuine), On the Holy Spirit, nine homilies on the six days of creation (the Hexaemeron), books against Eunomius, the monastic Rules (55 longer and 313 shorter), the Morals, many sermons, and the Address to Young Men on reading Greek literature.
wrote.source: Jackson, Introduction to the Letters: 'Of Saint Basil the extant letters, according to popular ascription, number three hundred and sixty-six. Of these three hundred and twenty-five, or, according to some, only three hundred and nineteen are genuine.' Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 116: 'composed admirable carefully written books Against Eunomius, a volume On the Holy Spirit, and nine homilies On the six days of creation'. Clarke 1925, introduction: 'the 55 Longer and 313 Shorter Rules' (OCR prints 813; the last heading is CCCXIII).
wrote.note: The Liturgy of St Basil is attributed to him; the Catholic Encyclopedia says 'its connexion with Basil has been a matter of critical discussion'. Do not list it plainly as something he wrote.

pronounced.text: BAY-zil the Great (also BAZ-il). Caesarea is see-zuh-REE-uh.
pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster gives BAY- first, then BAZ-, and an s sound as a third option. The respelling is mine from their IPA-style key.

roles.name: Student
roles.line: At Athens, with his friend Gregory
roles.note: Jackson dates his return to Caesarea to 356.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: In Pontus, by the river Iris
roles.source: Oration 43, sections 29 and 62; Letter 223, section 2; Jackson's table (358, 'retires to the monastery on the Iris'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('These Rules became the foundation for all Orthodox Christian monastic discipline')
roles.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "and wrote the Rules" dropped from the Monk role. Clarke (1925) thinks the Shorter Rules "probably date from B.'s episcopate"; the Rules cannot be pinned to the years in Pontus.

roles.name: Priest
roles.source: Jackson's chronological table ('364 ... Basil ordained priest by Eusebius'); OCA; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('ordained as a priest in 364')
roles.note: Oration 43, section 27: reader, then presbyter, then bishop.

roles.name: Bishop
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('In 370 Basil succeeded to the See of Caesarea, being consecrated according to tradition on 14 June'); Jackson's table (370, 379)
roles.note: As bishop of Caesarea he was metropolitan of Cappadocia (Catholic Encyclopedia; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022).

catholic.text: 2 January, a memorial shared with Gregory Nazianzen ('Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, Bishops and Doctors of the Church'). The 1916 Roman Martyrology kept his feast on 14 June, the traditional day he was made bishop, and noted his death on 1 January.
catholic.source: USCCB readings page for 2 January 2026 (Wayback capture; the live page blocks scripts), title 'Memorial of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, Bishops and Doctors of the Church'. 1916 Roman Martyrology, 1 January: 'At Caesarea, in Cappadocia, the demise of St. Basil, bishop, whose festival is kept on the 14th of June, the date of his consecration as bishop.' 14 June: 'At Caesarea, in Cappadocia, the consecration of St. Basil, bishop and doctor of the Church, who was eminent for learning and wisdom in the time of the emperor Valens.'
catholic.note: Why 2 January in today's calendar is not stated in any source I fetched (1 January is the Solemnity of Mary in the Roman calendar, but no document was read that gives that as the reason). The current (2004) Roman Martyrology was not checked.

orthodox.text: 1 January, the day he died (Greek churches, OCA and GOARCH). The Russian Church keeps 1 January on the old calendar, which is 14 January on the civil calendar. He is also honoured on 30 January with the Three Holy Hierarchs (12 February civil, on the old calendar).
orthodox.source: OCA life, 'Commemorated on January 1'; OCA, 30 January, 'Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs'; GOARCH (Wayback capture 2 December 2025; the live page blocks scripts): feast days 'January 1' and 'January 30'; azbyka.ru: 'Дни памяти 14 января 12 февраля - Собор Трех святителей'
orthodox.note: Unlike Martin, the Eastern churches agree on the day: 1 January. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'In the Greek Menaea he is commemorated on 1 January, the day of his death.' The Three Hierarchs feast: the Catholic Encyclopedia says it was set up in 1081 by 'John, Patriarch of Constantinople'; its own 1909 'Doctors of the Church' article says John, Bishop of Euchaita, under Alexius Comnenus (1081 to 1118). The two articles disagree on John's see; say 'in the eleventh century' (OCA: 'During the eleventh century, disputes raged in Constantinople about which of the three hierarchs was the greatest').

anglican.text: Church of England: 2 January, 'Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus, Bishops, Teachers of the Faith, 379 and 389', a Lesser Festival. The Episcopal Church: 14 June, 'Basil of Caesarea, Bishop and Theologian, 379'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in roman type, which the page's key defines as a Lesser Festival); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, June
anglican.note: The Episcopal Church keeps Gregory of Nazianzus on a different day (not checked).

lutheran.text: Missouri Synod (LCMS): 10 January, 'Basil the Great of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, Pastors and Confessors'. ELCA: 14 June, 'Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea, 379', with Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory of Nazianzus and Macrina.
lutheran.source: Concordia Publishing House (the LCMS publisher), 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations', from Lutheran Service Book pp. xii-xiii; Evangelical Lutheran Worship, 'The Church Year' (assembly version, 2006, via Wayback)
lutheran.note: The ELCA source is the 2006 pre-publication PDF of ELW's calendar (the same one used for Martin), not a current ELCA page.

why_they_differ.text: The Greek calendar keeps 1 January, the day of his death. The old Western calendars kept 14 June, the traditional day he was made bishop.
why_they_differ.source: Jackson, Prolegomena, note 299: 'In the Greek Kalendar January 1, the day of the death, is observed in honour of the saint. In the West St. Basil's day is June 14, the traditional date of the consecration.' Catholic Encyclopedia: the first Latin mention is by Usuard and Ado, 'who place it on 14 June, the supposed date of Basil's consecration'.
why_they_differ.note: 1 January is also New Year's Day, so in Greece gifts come from 'Agios Vasilis' and the Vasilopita is cut (see misquoted_or_legend).

numbers.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina: 'Eight years after this, the world-renowned Basil departed from men to live with God'; GOARCH: 'which he tended for eight years'
numbers.note: Consecrated 370 (by tradition 14 June), died 1 January 379: eight and a half years.
numbers.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page now cites GOARCH only ("which he tended for eight years"). In the Life of Macrina "Eight years after this" counts from Peter's ordination, not from Basil's consecration.

numbers.source: GOARCH: 'departed to the Lord on the 1st of January, in 379. at the age of forty-nine'
numbers.note: Follows from a birth in 329. If he died in 377 or 378, as some scholars hold, he was younger.
numbers.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "Worn out by illness" rests on Jackson, Prolegomena ("prematurely worn out with work and bad health"); GOARCH says "spent with extreme ascetical practices and continual labours". Both now cited.

numbers.source: Jackson, Introduction to the Letters, NPNF 2-8
numbers.note: Exact: 'three hundred and sixty-six. Of these three hundred and twenty-five, or, according to some, only three hundred and nineteen are genuine.'

numbers.source: Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (1925), introduction: 'the 55 Longer and 313 Shorter Rules'
numbers.note: Each rule answers a monk's question. OCR prints '813'; the last Shorter Rule heading is CCCXIII.

numbers.source: Jackson, Prolegomena; OCA life ('Five of them were later numbered among the saints')

Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 116 ('nine homilies On the six days of creation'); Jackson, Introduction to the Hexaemeron: 'They are Lenten sermons, delivered at both the morning and evening services, and appear to have been listened to by working men.'

traits.title: unafraid of power
traits.text: The emperor's prefect threatened him with 'Confiscation, banishment, torture, death.' Basil said none of them could touch him. He owned only rags and a few books, the whole earth was God's, and death would send him to God sooner. The prefect said no one had ever spoken to him like that. Basil answered: 'Why, perhaps, you have not met with a Bishop.'
traits.quote_exact: Why, perhaps," said Basil, "you have not met with a Bishop
traits.source: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43, sections 49 and 50
traits.note: The prefect is named in 50: 'No one has ever yet spoken thus, and with such boldness, to Modestus.' Sozomen (Church History 6.16) has Basil say 'I possess nothing but a cloak and a few books.'

traits.title: hands-on with the poor
traits.text: In a terrible famine he got the rich to open their stores. Then he gathered the hungry, set out 'basins of soup', and served them himself with his own servants. Gregory, who knew him best, calls him 'the poorest and most needy man whom I have known'.
traits.quote_exact: set before them basins of soup and such meat as was found preserved among us, on which the poor live.
traits.note: Jackson dates the famine to 368, when Basil was still a priest.

traits.title: stern, and taken for proud
traits.text: Some called him proud. Gregory answered that 'what they term pride is, I fancy, the firmness and steadfastness and stability of his character.' He was sparing with approval: 'His very smile often amounted to praise, his silence to rebuke.' Yet in private, Gregory asks, 'Who was more kindly in his stories, more refined in his wit, more tender in his rebukes?'
traits.quote_exact: His very smile often amounted to praise, his silence to rebuke

traits.title: hard on himself
traits.text: He lived on bread and salt, with one coat, a worn cloak and a bed on the bare ground. When an official threatened to have him torn with iron combs, he joked that it would cure his liver, 'which, as you see, is wearing me away.' Of his first retreat he admitted: 'I have not yet been able to get quit of myself.'
traits.quote_exact: I have abandoned my life in town, as one sure to lead to countless ills; but I have not yet been able to get quit of myself.
traits.source: Oration 43, sections 57 and 61; Basil, Letter 2, section 1
traits.note: Oration 43.61 exact: 'Hence came his single coat and well worn cloak, and his bed on the bare ground, his vigils, his unwashedness'. The liver line is 43.57.

others_on_him.lede: Almost everything we know about his life comes from his friend Gregory of Nazianzus, who gave his funeral speech, and from his brother Gregory of Nyssa.

quotes.exact: he is a glory to the Church
quotes.who: Athanasius of Alexandria, in 372, defending Basil against monks who complained about him
quotes.source: Athanasius, Letter 63, to the presbyter Palladius (Robertson, NPNF 2-4)
quotes.note: Same letter: 'glorify the Lord Who has given such a bishop to Cappadocia as any district must pray to have.' Robertson's note says the monks objected to 'the reserve with which he spoke of the Divine Personality of the Holy Spirit'. The letter's date (372) is from the NPNF chronology list ('372: *Letters to John and Antiochus and to Palladius (62, 63)').

quotes.exact: We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.
quotes.who: Gregory of Nazianzus, on their student days at Athens
quotes.note: Much searched ('basil and gregory friendship'). Already on the personality test's opposite panel.

quotes.exact: Basil, our common father and teacher
quotes.who: Gregory of Nyssa, his younger brother
quotes.source: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man, dedication to his brother Peter (Wilson, NPNF 2-5)
quotes.note: Nyssa wrote this to finish Basil's Hexaemeron.

quotes.exact: He was puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory and looked down on the local dignitaries, excelling in his own estimation all the men of leading and position.
quotes.who: Gregory of Nyssa, on Basil coming home from university
quotes.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina (Clarke 1916), section headed 'Basil returns from the University'
quotes.note: The honest one. Good for the 'life in moments' section rather than here.

life_moments.title: One soul in two bodies
life_moments.text: At Athens he met again his friend Gregory, from Nazianzus. Gregory made sure the older students did not haze him. The two lived together and knew only two roads: one to church and one to their teachers. Parties and theatres they left to others.
life_moments.source: Oration 43, sections 15 to 21 (21: 'Two ways were known to us ... the one leading to our sacred buildings and the teachers there, the other to secular instructors. All others we left to those who would pursue them — to feasts, theatres, meetings, banquets.')
life_moments.note: Section 16: Gregory says he got the other students to spare Basil the usual ragging, so 'he was the only one to escape the general rule'. Jackson's table has him back in Caesarea in 356.

life_moments.title: The proud young speaker
life_moments.text: He came home a star of public speaking, and proud of it. His older sister Macrina took him in hand. He gave up his career and his property. In his own words, he woke 'like a man roused from deep sleep'. He wept over his life and went to see the monks of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia.
life_moments.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina ('Basil returns from the University'); Basil, Letter 223, section 2
life_moments.note: Letter 223 exact: 'Then once upon a time, like a man roused from deep sleep, I turned my eyes to the marvellous light of the truth of the Gospel'; 'I wept many tears over my miserable life'. Basil's own letter does not mention Macrina; the Life of Macrina does. Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 adds the death of 'a beloved younger brother' (Naucratius) as a cause.

life_moments.title: The famine
life_moments.text: A famine struck, the worst anyone remembered. Merchants hoarded grain to drive up prices. Basil preached until the rich opened their stores. Then he gathered the hungry of every age, set out basins of soup, and with his own servants waited on them, the way Christ washed His disciples' feet.
life_moments.source: Oration 43, sections 34 to 36; Jackson's table ('368 ... Famine in Cappadocia')
life_moments.note: 43.35: 'imitating the ministry of Christ, Who, girded with a towel, did not disdain to wash the disciples' feet'.

life_moments.title: The prefect and the emperor
life_moments.text: The emperor Valens favoured the Arians and wanted Basil to conform. His prefect Modestus threatened Basil with every penalty, and failed. He told the emperor, 'We have been worsted, Sire, by the prelate of this Church.' On the feast of Epiphany Valens came to Basil's church. The singing and Basil's stillness so shook him that he staggered, and someone had to steady him.
life_moments.source: Oration 43, sections 48 to 53; Jackson's table (371, Modestus; 372, 'Valens attends great service at Caesarea on the Epiphany, Jan. 6')
life_moments.note: Gregory never names Valens in the speech ('the Anti-Christian Emperor'); Theodoret (4.16) and Sozomen (6.16) do. 43.52: Basil stood 'as if, so to say, he had been a statue'.

life_moments.title: The new city
life_moments.text: He built what Gregory calls 'the new city' just outside Caesarea. It had lodging for travellers and care for the sick, with doctors and nurses. Lepers, driven out of towns, were nursed there. Basil, a nobleman, greeted them as brothers and kissed them.
life_moments.source: Oration 43, sections 63 and 64; Basil, Letter 94, to Elias ('a place of entertainment for strangers, both for those who are on a journey and for those who require medical treatment on account of sickness ... physicians, doctors, means of conveyance, and escort')
life_moments.note: Later called the Basileias (name not in these sources; do not print it as ancient without a source). Theodoret 4.16 says Valens gave 'some fine lands which he had there for the poor under his care'. Jackson's table: 'Valens endows Ptochotrophium'.

life_moments.title: A bishopric for his best friend
life_moments.text: The province was split in two, and a rival bishop claimed half of Basil's churches. To hold his ground, Basil made new bishops. He made Gregory bishop of Sasima, a small posting station on the disputed road. Gregory never forgave it. He wrote to Basil, 'Give me before all things quiet.' Years later, in his funeral speech, he still called it 'a cause of pain which even time has not obliterated.'
life_moments.source: Oration 43, sections 58 and 59; Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 48; Jackson's table (372)
life_moments.note: 43.59: 'I am afraid that I myself was treated as an appendage to this scheme.' 'Small posting station': the NPNF 2-7 editors call Sasima 'a miserable little village'; Gregory's Letter 48 speaks of 'the celebrated Sasima' with sarcasm. Say 'a small village'. The rival was Anthimus of Tyana (43.58 does not name him; Letter 50 does).
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the draft said Anthimus "claimed half of Basil's churches". No source says half. Oration 43.58: the new metropolitan "claimed those newly added, as belonging to him"; Jackson: Anthimus, bishop of Tyana, "contended that an ecclesiastical partition should follow the civil". Page now: "claimed the churches of the new half for himself".

life_moments.title: A book about the Spirit
life_moments.text: Praying with his people, he gave glory to the Father 'with the Son together with the Holy Ghost', and some people attacked him for it. His young friend Amphilochius asked him to explain. The answer was On the Holy Spirit. It argues that the Spirit shares the Father's and the Son's glory.
life_moments.source: On the Holy Spirit, chapter 1, section 3; Jackson's table ('374 ... Basil writes the "De Spiritu Sancto"'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
life_moments.note: Exact: 'Lately when praying with the people, and using the full doxology to God the Father in both forms, at one time "with the Son together with the Holy Ghost," and at another "through the Son in the Holy Ghost," I was attacked by some of those present'.
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page prints "About 374", the year Jackson's table gives ("374 ... Basil writes the De Spiritu Sancto"), not "About 375".

miracles.lede: Gregory says Basil could not "rain bread from heaven by prayer", as Moses did in the wilderness. But he tells of healings, and of wonders when Basil was made bishop and when he died.

lede_quote.exact: He indeed could neither rain bread from heaven by prayer

items.title: The emperor's son
items.text: The order to exile Basil was signed and his carriage stood ready. That night the emperor's small son fell ill with a fever. The doctors could do nothing, and Valens lay on the floor in grief. He sent friends to fetch Basil. When Basil came, the fever eased at once. But Valens also called in Arian clergy, and the boy died.
items.quote_exact: On his arrival, without the delay or reluctance which any one else might have shown, at once the disease relaxed, and the father cherished better hopes
items.witness: Gregory says the boy would have lived had Valens not 'blended salt water with the fresh' by trusting the heretics too, and adds: 'This indeed was the conviction of those who were present at the time, and shared in the distress.'
items.source: Oration 43, section 54; Sozomen, Church History 6.16 ('Immediately on the arrival of Basil, the boy began to rally'); Theodoret, Church History 4.16
items.note: The boy's name, Galates, is in Socrates 4.26 and Sozomen 6.16. Theodoret's version: Basil promised the boy's life if he were baptised by the orthodox; Valens had Arians baptise him, 'who immediately died'.

items.title: The prefect
items.text: Modestus, the prefect who had threatened Basil, fell ill in his turn. In tears he sent for Basil and begged, 'I own that you were in the right; only save me!' He recovered, and afterwards he never stopped telling people what Basil could do.
items.quote_exact: I own that you were in the right; only save me!
items.witness: Gregory: 'His request was granted, as he himself acknowledged, and convinced many who had known nothing of it'. But he opens with 'is said to have'.
items.source: Oration 43, section 55; Sozomen, Church History 6.16 ('It is said that the prefect, likewise, fell ill; but that on his repentance, and on prayer being offered to God, he was restored to health.')

items.title: The old bishop in the litter
items.text: When Basil was chosen bishop, Gregory's father, the aged bishop of Nazianzus, came to vote and help consecrate him. He was so ill he was carried in a litter 'as a corpse is laid in its tomb'. He went home, says his son, 'in the freshness and strength of youth, with head erect'.
items.quote_exact: he was placed in his litter, as a corpse is laid in its tomb, to return in the freshness and strength of youth, with head erect
items.witness: Gregory of Nazianzus, about his own father.
items.note: Gregory credits the Spirit and 'the head of him who was anointed' (Basil). It is a wonder around Basil rather than one he worked.

items.title: Strength on his deathbed
items.text: Almost dead and barely breathing, he grew stronger in his last words, long enough to ordain the best of his disciples as priests. Gregory calls it 'a wonder in no wise inferior to those mentioned before'.
items.quote_exact: he grew stronger in his last words, so as to depart with the utterances of religion
items.witness: Gregory, who was not there (Letter 76: he was too ill to come).

items.title: Three broken pens
items.text: Later Valens again signed an order to exile Basil. But the pen broke. A second pen broke, and a third. His hand shook, and he tore the order up with both hands.
items.quote_exact: for the pen broke, and when the same thing happened to the second and to the third pen, and he still strove to sign that wicked edict, his hand shook
items.witness: No witness named. Theodoret wrote his history about 438 to 439, some sixty years after Basil's death.
items.source: Theodoret, Church History, Book 4, chapter 16 (Jackson, NPNF 2-3); dating from Jackson's note 936
items.note: Gregory and Sozomen do not tell it. GOARCH tells it today. Mark it as the later telling it is.

doubt.title: The sources disagree
doubt.text: Socrates, writing about sixty years later, tells the story of the emperor's son with no healing at all. Basil says only that God's will concerning the child will be done, and the child dies. Sozomen says only that 'many maintain' the boy would have recovered. Even Gregory says the prefect's illness 'is said to have' happened.

quotes.exact: God's will concerning the child will be done then
the child, however, died shortly after.
The same mischance is said to have befallen the prefect.

doubt.note: Sozomen exact: 'so that many maintain that his recovery would have been complete' (in the saved Sozomen text). The date of Socrates's history (about 439) is from general knowledge, not a fetched page: say 'writing two generations later' or check the NPNF 2-2 introduction.

later_legends.title: Mercurius and the emperor Julian
later_legends.text: A medieval story says Basil saw in a vision the martyr Mercurius sent to kill the emperor Julian. In the morning Mercurius's spear in his tomb was bloody, and word came that Julian had died in battle.
later_legends.quote_exact: found the body and the armour and the spear all bloody
later_legends.source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine, about 1260; Caxton's English, ed. Ellis 1900), in its lives of the saints named Julian; its life of Basil says it follows 'Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium'. Catholic Encyclopedia: 'The Vita Basilii by AMPHILOCHIUS is a forgery of about the ninth century.'
later_legends.note: Julian died in 363, when Basil was not yet a bishop. None of the fourth- or fifth-century sources I read tell this.

later_legends.title: Ephrem's vision
later_legends.text: The same late Life says the Syrian hermit Ephrem saw Basil as a pillar of fire, came to Caesarea to see him, and said, 'Truly Basil is great, truly Basil is the pillar of fire'.
later_legends.quote_exact: Truly Basil is great, truly Basil is the pillar of fire
later_legends.source: The Golden Legend, Life of St Basil (Ellis 1900)
later_legends.note: From the forged Life. The Golden Legend also gets his death wrong: 'about the year of our Lord three hundred and seventy'.

miracles.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the lede's "healings that the people there believed in" and the pens item's "Theodoret wrote about sixty years after Basil died. Gregory does not tell this story" hedged the miracles in our voice (the owner's rule). Removed; the doubts stay in "The sources disagree", in the sources' own words. Sozomen corrected there: he does say the boy "began to rally" when Basil came, and gives only the full recovery as what "many maintain that his recovery would have been complete".

framing.text: Basil wrote a great deal that survives: letters, sermons, treatises and Rules for monks. These are his own words, in public-domain translations.
framing.note: Some letters under his name are not his: Jackson says only about 325 of 366 are genuine. Avoid Letter 8 (usually given to Evagrius), Letter 38 (perhaps Gregory of Nyssa), the letters to Apollinarius, and Letter 46 'To a fallen virgin' (disputed). Research note, not independently checked beyond Jackson's count.

feature.exact: Whose feet then wilt thou wash ? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
feature.display: Whose feet then wilt thou wash? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
feature.ctx: Arguing that monks should live together, not as hermits. Just before, he says Christ 'girded Himself and washed the feet of the disciples in person.'
feature.source: Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (1925)
feature.note: The OCR prints a space before the first question mark. Clarke's heading for Rule 7: 'That it is necessary, with a view to pleasing God, to live with like-minded persons, and that solitude is difficult and dangerous.' The Greek was not found in a readable free copy (the PG PDF on khazarzar.skeptik.net uses a broken font), so no Greek is given. Ghost word idea: 'feet'.

lines.exact: Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God, for Whom I live, and exist, and have all but died, and to Whom I have long been hastening.
lines.display: Death is my benefactor, for it will send me the sooner to God, for Whom I live, and exist, and have all but died, and to Whom I have long been hastening.
lines.ctx: To the prefect Modestus, who had threatened him with death. As Gregory of Nazianzus reports it.

lines.exact: Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labour which I underwent in acquiring the wisdom made foolish by God. Then once upon a time, like a man roused from deep sleep, I turned my eyes to the marvellous light of the truth of the Gospel
lines.display: Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labour which I underwent in acquiring the wisdom made foolish by God. Then once upon a time, like a man roused from deep sleep, I turned my eyes to the marvellous light of the truth of the Gospel
lines.ctx: Looking back on his turn to Christ, in a letter written about twenty years later.

lines.exact: We have not lost the lad; we have restored him to the Lender.
lines.display: We have not lost the lad; we have restored him to the Lender.
lines.ctx: To his friend Nectarius, whose son, the heir of the house, had just died in the bloom of manhood.
lines.note: Section 1 describes the son: 'heir of a noble house, prop of a family, a father's hope ... in the very bloom of manhood'. Not 'only son'.

lines.exact: For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense.
lines.display: For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense.
lines.ctx: Preaching on the days of creation, against those who turned everything in Genesis into symbols.
lines.note: Do not recruit him for either side of modern creation debates: in the same section he declines to say what shape the earth is, because Moses is silent.

lines.exact: I want creation to penetrate you with so much admiration that everywhere, wherever you may be, the least plant may bring to you the clear remembrance of the Creator.
lines.display: I want creation to penetrate you with so much admiration that everywhere, wherever you may be, the least plant may bring to you the clear remembrance of the Creator.
lines.ctx: To his congregation, on the third day of creation.

lines.exact: But to whom do we do any harm by building a place of entertainment for strangers, both for those who are on a journey and for those who require medical treatment on account of sickness
lines.display: But to whom do we do any harm by building a place of entertainment for strangers, both for those who are on a journey and for those who require medical treatment on account of sickness
lines.ctx: To the provincial governor, answering complaints about his building works outside Caesarea.
lines.work: Letter 94, to Elias, governor of the province
lines.place: the whole letter is one section

lines.exact: But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable ; so that we praise God with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs while we move our hands in work
lines.display: But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable; so that we praise God with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs while we move our hands in work
lines.ctx: To monks who skipped work 'under pretext of prayers and psalmody'.

lines.exact: Harshness is ever to be put aside, even in censuring.
lines.display: Harshness is ever to be put aside, even in censuring.
lines.ctx: Advice to his friend Gregory on how to speak to others.

lines.exact: The bread you are holding on to belongs to the hungry. The cloak you guard in your storerooms belongs to the naked.
lines.display: The bread you are holding on to belongs to the hungry. The cloak you guard in your storerooms belongs to the naked.
lines.ctx: To the rich of Caesarea, in a sermon on the rich fool who planned bigger barns. Our translation.
lines.work: Homily on 'I will pull down my barns'
lines.note: OUR translation, already on the site (quiz cell 'surplus'). Greek, read in the fetched text: 'Τοῦ πεινῶντός ἐστιν ὁ ἄρτος, ὃν σὺ κατέχεις· τοῦ γυμνητεύοντος τὸ ἱμάτιον, ὃ σὺ φυλάσσεις ἐν ἀποθήκαις'. It is his most searched line. It may only appear labelled 'Our translation'; ask the owner if that is acceptable on the saint page, since the brief says public-domain translations. The section number 7 is from the research; the free Greek copy has no numbers.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'O God, enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all living things, our brothers the animals...' (the 'Prayer of St Basil' for animals)
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his. It is from Walter Rauschenbusch's prayer 'For This World', in Prayers of the Social Awakening (Boston, 1910).
misquoted_or_legend.exact_evidence: Enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all the living things, our little brothers, to whom thou hast given this earth as their home in common with us.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Rauschenbusch, Prayers of the Social Awakening (1910), 'For This World', pp. 46 to 48 (archive.org OCR)
misquoted_or_legend.note: The popular Basil version rewords it ('our brothers the animals'). The claim that the wording also blends a First World War prayer for horses is in the fathers research and on animalsmattertogod.com; I did not check that part.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'The bread you store up belongs to the hungry; the coat hanging in your closet belongs to the naked; the shoes rotting in your closet belong to the barefoot; the money in your vaults belongs to the destitute.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Really his in substance, from his sermon on the rich fool's barns. But the wording is a loose modern paraphrase: there are no closets or vaults in the Greek. The shoes are there: 'the shoe that is rotting with you'. The money is 'the silver you have buried'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Basil, Homily on 'I will pull down my barns' (PG 31), Greek text fetched: 'τοῦ ἀνυποδέτου τὸ ὑπόδημα, ὃ παρὰ σοὶ κατασήπεται· τοῦ χρῄζοντος τὸ ἀργύριον, ὃ κατορύξας ἔχεις'
misquoted_or_legend.note: The English glosses of the Greek are mine.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "The Greek has no closets" is too strong: the cloak is kept "ἐν ἀποθήκαις", in storerooms (the site's own translation says "storerooms"). Page now: "In the Greek the cloak is kept in storerooms, not hanging in a closet, and there are no vaults."

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'A tree is known by its fruit; a man by his deeds. A good deed is never lost; he who sows courtesy reaps friendship, and he who plants kindness gathers love.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Quote sites give no source. It is not in his letters, On the Holy Spirit, the Hexaemeron, the Rules or the Address to Young Men.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Script search of the fetched texts (Jackson NPNF 2-8, Clarke 1925, Padelford 1902) for 'courtesy', 'good deed is never lost', 'plants kindness', 'known by its fruit': no hits
misquoted_or_legend.note: Absence in the translated works is real evidence but not proof: many of his sermons have no public-domain English. Print as 'We could not find it in his writings, and the sites that quote it give no source', or leave it out.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He hid gold coins in a loaf and gave them back to the people of Caesarea, each finding their own. This is the origin of the Vasilopita, the New Year cake with a coin in it.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A pious story, and Greek Orthodox parishes tell it as one. It is not in Gregory's funeral speech or the church historians. The real Basil did write to officials to ease taxes, for example asking the prefect Modestus to keep clergy exempt from the new census.
misquoted_or_legend.exact_evidence: For centuries upon centuries parents, grandparents and godparents have related the following pious story to Orthodox children about Saint Basil and the Vasilopita.
misquoted_or_legend.source: St. Andrew Greek Orthodox Church, 'The Orthodox Tradition of the Vasilopita' (2015); script search of Oration 43, Socrates 4.26, Sozomen 6.16, Theodoret 4.16 for tax, coin, jewel, loaf, cake: no hits; Basil, Letter 104 ('By the old census, the clergy of God, presbyters and deacons, were left exempt.')
misquoted_or_legend.note: When the story first appears in writing is not checked.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Stories of Basil and the emperor Julian, Mercurius's spear, Ephrem's vision, the Jewish doctor Joseph, the woman whose written sins vanished.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: From a Life said to be by his friend Amphilochius. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it 'a forgery of about the ninth century'. The medieval Golden Legend spread these stories, and even gets his death wrong ('about the year of our Lord three hundred and seventy').
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907); The Golden Legend, Life of St Basil (Ellis 1900)

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He wrote the Divine Liturgy of St Basil.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: It bears his name and is still used on ten days a year in Orthodox churches. How much of it is his own has long been argued. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'its connexion with Basil has been a matter of critical discussion'.
misquoted_or_legend.note: 'Ten days a year' is from a web search summary of Greek sources, NOT checked in a church document: drop it or verify. Modern scholarship (Capelle, Fenwick) that credits Basil with revising the anaphora was not read.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He studied under Libanius at Antioch with Gregory (Socrates says so). He was made bishop by Meletius of Antioch (Socrates).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Socrates is muddled here. Gregory, who was there, puts their studies at Athens, and Basil was consecrated at Caesarea after the death of its bishop Eusebius, with Gregory's own father voting.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Socrates, Church History 4.26; Oration 43, sections 14 to 22 and 37
misquoted_or_legend.note: GOARCH says he 'studied in Constantnople under the sophist Libanius' (Constantinople, not Antioch). Low priority; include only if the page needs a sixth item.

where_he_stood.text: Twelve of the quiz's 23 statements show a line of his (two more, 'nature' and 'pure', are on record but hidden). Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.basil.cells). Ten are word for word in public-domain translations. Two ('rich', 'surplus') are the site's own translations from the Greek.

rows.place: Rule 31, 'Must we not laugh at all?' (Clarke 1925, p. 241)
rows.line: Since the Lord condemns those that laugh it is obvious that there is never a time of laughter for the believer.
rows.note: Cut short: the sentence goes on 'especially when there is so great a multitude of those who ... are dead in sins, for whom one should mourn and grieve.' Written for monks. In Longer Rule 17 he allows 'a cheerful smile' but not loud laughter. The page must say both.

rows.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
rows.line: So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest.
rows.note: Padelford 1902. His outline puts the discriminating reader under chapter IV.

rows.work: Homily against Anger (Homily 10, Against the Angry)
rows.place: quoted in Jackson's Prolegomena, NPNF 2-8, 'The Homilies'
rows.line: Anger, stirred at the proper time and in the proper manner, is an efficient cause of manliness, patience, and endurance.
rows.note: Jackson quotes it without a section number (the research said section 6: not checked). Shorter Rule 29 is harsher on anger; do not present the homily as his only view.

rows.line: Whose feet then wilt thou wash? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
rows.note: His LATER view. About 358, in Letter 2, section 2, he praised solitude: 'Now solitude is of the greatest use for this purpose, inasmuch as it stills our passions'. A real change of mind; say so.

rows.work: Homily to the Rich (Homilia in divites)
rows.line: So the more you abound in wealth, the more you fall short in love.
rows.note: OUR translation. Greek fetched: 'Ὅσον οὖν πλεονάζεις τῷ πλούτῳ, τοσοῦτον ἐλλείπεις τῇ ἀγάπῃ. (Homilia in divites PG 31,281)'. Faithful. 'section 1' is from the research, not a numbered edition.

rows.line: Those who pretend to be kind (really suffering from the disease of men-pleasing) and fail to rebuke sinners, are actually sentencing them.
rows.note: Clarke's sentence goes on 'and laying plots against their true life' (OCR 'lofe'). The site ends it at 'them' with a full stop. Clarke abbreviates the Morals.

rows.work: Letter to the wife of Arinthaeus the general
rows.line: Be an example of fortitude to other women, and so regulate your grief that you may neither eject it from your heart, nor be overwhelmed by your distress.

rows.place: Rule 76, 'Is it lawful to lie in order to achieve some supposed good?' (Clarke 1925, p. 259)
rows.line: It is forbidden by the decision of the Lord Who said once for all that lying is of the devil, and allowed no difference in lying.
rows.note: Read by eye: the OCR prints 'It 1s' and a stray mark after 'devil,'. Otherwise word for word.

rows.work: Homily on 'I will pull down my barns'
rows.line: The bread you are holding on to belongs to the hungry. The cloak you guard in your storerooms belongs to the naked.
rows.note: OUR translation, faithful to the Greek (see his_words). Section number unverified in a numbered edition.

rows.line: There are those truly, who do not admit the common sense of the Scriptures, for whom water is not water, but some other nature
rows.note: The next sentences: 'For me grass is grass'. Scope: this is about the creation account; elsewhere he reads Scripture morally.

rows.line: So he who is seized by the vehement desire of following Christ can no longer care for anything to do with this life.
But if we cannot think this of life, with what reason shall we give eternal punishment an end? For both equally have the adjective eternal.
rows.note: The page header is printed '880' in the OCR (p. 330). His brother Gregory of Nyssa leaned the other way; the hub's Nyssa page covers that.

friends_family_rivals.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
friends_family_rivals.text: His closest friend from their student days at Athens. They fell out when Basil made him bishop of Sasima, and Gregory still gave the great speech at his funeral.
friends_family_rivals.note: Or 43.14: Basil 'had not been unknown to me before' Athens. OCA says they first met at the schools of Caesarea.

friends_family_rivals.name: Macrina the Younger
friends_family_rivals.text: The eldest of the ten children. When he came home proud of his speaking, she turned him to a life of prayer and work.
friends_family_rivals.note: Basil never mentions her in his surviving writings (a known oddity; not checked against every letter, so do not print it without checking).
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "turned him to prayer and work" is not the source's wording. Life of Macrina: she drew him "toward the mark of philosophy" and he "deserted it for this busy life where one toils with one's hands". Page: "she drew him to the monk's life, working with his hands".

friends_family_rivals.name: Gregory of Nyssa
friends_family_rivals.text: Basil made him bishop of Nyssa. He also scolded him for forging letters from their uncle to patch up a quarrel: 'who ever falls a third time into the same nets?'
friends_family_rivals.source: Basil, Letter 58; Jackson's table (372, 'consecrates his brother Gregory to Nyssa')
friends_family_rivals.note: Letter 58 exact: 'You forged one letter, and brought it me as though it came from our right reverend uncle the bishop, trying to deceive me, I have no idea why.'

friends_family_rivals.name: Peter of Sebaste
friends_family_rivals.text: Basil ordained him priest. Peter later became bishop of Sebaste.
friends_family_rivals.source: Life of Macrina ('He advanced Peter to the sacred order of the priesthood'); 1916 Martyrology, 9 January
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: bishop of Sebaste rests on Jackson ("the sees of Caesarea, Nyssa, and Sebasteia"), now cited beside the Life of Macrina.

friends_family_rivals.name: Emmelia and Basil the Elder
friends_family_rivals.text: His father, also Basil, was a lawyer and teacher of rhetoric in Pontus. His mother Emmelia was the daughter of a martyr.
friends_family_rivals.source: Jackson, Prolegomena; OCA life ('Saint Emilia was the daughter of a martyr')
friends_family_rivals.note: Life of Macrina: 'Our maternal grandfather was slain by the imperial wrath'. The OCA Emilia URL was seen as a link on the 1 January page, not opened.

friends_family_rivals.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
friends_family_rivals.text: The old defender of Nicaea stood up for Basil when monks at Caesarea attacked him, calling him 'a glory to the Church'.
friends_family_rivals.note: Basil wrote him several letters (Letters 66, 67, 69, 80, 82 in NPNF): titles not individually checked.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Athanasius wrote this to Palladius, not to the monks (his letter to them is lost). Page: "Athanasius wrote that he was a glory to the Church, and that they should obey him".

friends_family_rivals.name: Eustathius of Sebasteia
friends_family_rivals.text: His early guide in the monastic life. They split over the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and in 375 Basil broke his silence to answer him.
friends_family_rivals.source: Basil, Letter 223 ('There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak'); Jackson's table (376, 'Open denunciation of Eustathius by Basil')
friends_family_rivals.note: Jackson's table says 376; Jackson places Letter 223 in 375. Say 'in the mid-370s'.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "early guide" softened to "an older monk he admired" (Jackson: Basil "relates in strong terms his admiration for the ascetic character of Eustathius"). The split over the Spirit rests on Jackson (the 373 creed with additions on the Macedonian controversy, which Eustathius signed and broke), not on Letter 223, so Jackson is now cited. Letter 223: "this is now the third year of my silence".

friends_family_rivals.name: Valens and Modestus
friends_family_rivals.text: The emperor and his prefect, who favoured the Arians and tried to bend Basil with threats. Both ended up respecting him.

friends_family_rivals.name: Anthimus of Tyana
friends_family_rivals.text: When Cappadocia was split, he claimed half of Basil's churches, and once blocked Basil's road and seized his mules.
friends_family_rivals.source: Oration 43, section 58 (the act, unnamed); Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 50 (names 'the most noble Anthimus'); NPNF 2-7 editors' note
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "claimed half of Basil's churches" corrected (no source says half). He was bishop of Tyana (Jackson).

friends_family_rivals.name: Pope Damasus and the Western bishops
friends_family_rivals.text: Basil begged the West for help against the Arians and grew bitter at its slowness: 'what help can come to us from the frown of the West?'
friends_family_rivals.source: Basil, Letter 239, to Eusebius of Samosata
friends_family_rivals.note: Same letter: 'Really lofty souls, when they are courted, get haughtier than ever.' Damasus is not named in that line; the NPNF note ties 'their Coryphaeus' to him (not checked).

how_he_died.text: He died at Caesarea on 1 January 379, about 49 years old, worn out by illness and hard living. Near death, he rallied long enough to ordain the best of his disciples. His last words were Christ's own, from the cross: 'Into Thy Hands I commend my spirit.' The whole city crowded round him. At the funeral, tens of thousands came, Jews and pagans too, and many were crushed to death.

last_words.exact: Into thy Hands I commend my spirit,
last_words.display: Into Thy Hands I commend my spirit.
last_words.note: Luke 23:46. 'Thy' is God: capital. 'my' is Basil: lower case.

how_he_died.source: Oration 43, sections 78 to 80 ('tens of thousands of every race and age, beyond all previous experience'; 'Our own people vied with strangers, Jews, Greeks, and foreigners'; 'many souls departed along with him, from the violence of the pushing and confusion'); GOARCH (age 49); Catholic Encyclopedia ('Jews, pagans, and foreigners vied with his own flock in doing him honour')
how_he_died.note: Gregory was not there. Letter 76, to Gregory of Nyssa: 'by reason of the bodily sickness from which I am still suffering and in great danger, I cannot kiss that holy dust'. The funeral speech (Oration 43) came later; its date (often put in 381 or 382) is not in any page I fetched. Gregory says Basil was 'almost dead, and breathless' (43.78). No cause beyond chronic illness is recorded; 'liver' is Basil's own joke (43.57), not a diagnosis of his death.

later.title: A later story
later.text: The Golden Legend, following the forged Life, says he stayed alive one more day to baptise a Jewish doctor named Joseph who had predicted his death that evening.
later.source: The Golden Legend, Life of St Basil (Ellis 1900)

how_he_died.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "some" corrected to "many" (Oration 43.80). The last words now link CCEL's NPNF page (https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf207.iii.xxvi.html), which prints "Into thy Hands"; New Advent's copy modernises it to "your".

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes. He was never condemned. Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church, the Orthodox one of the Three Holy Hierarchs, the Church of England keeps a Lesser Festival, and both big American Lutheran churches remember him.

churches.status: Saint and Doctor of the Church
churches.note: Memorial on 2 January, with Gregory Nazianzen
1 January, and 30 January with the Three Holy Hierarchs
Church of England, 2 January; Episcopal Church, 14 June

quote.exact: the consecration of St. Basil, bishop and doctor of the Church, who was eminent for learning and wisdom in the time of the emperor Valens. Being adorned with every virtue, he was a great light in the Church, and defended her with admirable constancy against the Arians and Macedonians.

prayer_he_wrote.text: Leave this section out. The prayers that carry his name (the Liturgy of St Basil, and prayers in the Orthodox prayer books) are traditionally his, but their authorship is debated. No prayer was found in his undisputed works that stands as a prayer on its own.

prayer_he_wrote.note: The Hexaemeron has short doxologies and a quoted psalm ('O Lord, how manifold are Thy works!', Homily 9), not a prayer of his own.

hub_card.groups_note: The hint was 'fathers cappadocians teachers'. I suggest adding 'monks': he founded monasteries in Pontus and wrote the Rules that Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 calls 'the foundation for all Orthodox Christian monastic discipline'; Gregory (Oration 43.62) credits him with uniting the hermit and community life. Martin, a founder of monasteries, is in 'monks'. Check how the hub defines 'monks' before adding. 'teachers' holds: a Doctor of the Church (USCCB) and one of the Three Hierarchs, 'Ecumenical Teachers' (OCA).
hub_card.note: Lived about 329 to 379, all in the Greek-speaking East (Cappadocia, Pontus, Constantinople, Athens). Both hints correct.

personality_test.text: The test names him twice. He is a kindred saint of The Herald ('Sure of yourself, and at your best when there is something to do'), labelled 'as a young man': 'His brother says Basil came home from university proud of his speaking. He looked down on the leading men of his town, until his sister Macrina turned him round.' And he is the Herald in the Herald and Still Water opposite pair, against Gregory the Theologian.
personality_test.note: Checked against the Life of Macrina: 'looked down on the local dignitaries' supports 'leading men of his town'. The opposite pair's story (Athens, Sasima, 'Give me before all things quiet', 'one soul, inhabiting two bodies') checks out against Oration 43 and Letter 48. Label it 'as a young man' on his page too: Gregory's portrait of the older Basil is of a man called proud but humble in deed. The live URL was not opened.

hard_topics.text: He accepted slavery. Runaway slaves who came to his monasteries were to be 'admonished and made better, and then restored' to their masters, as Paul sent Onesimus back. Only a master who ordered sin lost that claim.
hard_topics.note: OCR prints 'restored Dto their masters' (a margin letter). His brother Gregory of Nyssa preached against owning slaves at all (research claim; Homily 4 on Ecclesiastes; not checked here).
hard_topics.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "Only if a master ordered sin could the monks keep the slave" went beyond the Rule. Longer Rule 11 gives two courses for a master who orders sin: "preparing that slave to endure the sufferings that will be inflicted upon him", or "the acceptance by those who have received him of the troubles that may come upon them on his account".

hard_topics.text: He called a third marriage 'no longer described as marriage at all, but as polygamy; nay rather as limited fornication'. He was passing on older church rules, and he did impose penance on them.

For monks he wrote that 'there is never a time of laughter for the believer', since so many are dead in sin. Elsewhere he allows 'a cheerful smile' but not loud, shaking laughter. His friend Gregory remembered his 'refined' wit.
hard_topics.note: Say plainly these Rules were written for monks.

hard_topics.text: He made Gregory bishop of Sasima against his will to win a church quarrel. Gregory's word for how he was used: 'an appendage to this scheme'.

In public he avoided saying the plain words 'the Spirit is God', to keep the Arians from a pretext to exile him and seize his church. Monks attacked him for it. Gregory and Athanasius defended him: he believed it, Gregory says, and said it in private and often in preaching.
hard_topics.source: Oration 43, sections 68 and 69 ('The enemy were on the watch for the unqualified statement "the Spirit is God;"'); Athanasius, Letter 63 with Robertson's note
hard_topics.note: Critics then called it timidity; Gregory calls it 'economy'. Both views are in the sources.

hard_topics.text: He said killing in war is not murder, as earlier Fathers held, but advised that soldiers with blood on their hands stay from communion for three years.
hard_topics.note: 'Perhaps, however, it is well to counsel...': advice, not a hard rule.

checked_by_adversary.summary: Every claim on design/saints-hub/pages/basil-the-great.json re-read against the fetched primary texts and the churches' own calendars. Fixes are in the checker_note fields above and in the page. Also on the page: the lede, card line and "Who was Basil?" no longer say he fed the city in the famine AS BISHOP (Oration 43.35 to 37: the famine came while he was a priest; he was made bishop after it); Letter 58 retold exactly (Gregory forged the first letter and brought it; the second came "by the hands of your servant Asterius"); Letter 239 is about courting the West, not bishops "slow to help"; every "section N" shown to readers is now "chapter N".
